event: During LM source inspection of a fuel cell support kit, HLB SN 2-1619 and the solenoid test cable overheated and the battery control board was burned; no aircraft involved.
component: HLB 16-pin ODU connector solder cups (battery heater charge cable 114-105901)
failure_mode: intermittent short between ODU pins 8 and 9 (gray and violet wires) shorting cell 2, most likely a stray wire strand outside a solder cup, triggered by handling when the test harness was connected; overheated wiring and burned the battery control PCB
contributing: battery built October 2022 before electronics inspection of the solder cups was in place
ODU connector installed tilted, pressing the wires against the enclosure wall
no electrical test after potting

evidence.quote: Looks like the ODU pins 8 and 9 are shorted together, which would short out cell 2.
I tested the solenoid test cable using the cable tester and no shorts were found.
I was able to replicate the short by slightly wiggling the wires just behind the 16 pin ODU on the battery.
The gray and violet wires were the shorted connection but unfortunately it seems I removed the short when removing the potting.
there is high probability that a wire strand was outside the solder cup on the ODU and caused the intermittent short

team_root_cause:
Intermittent short in 16 pin ODU wiring inside the battery, pins 8 and 9. This would short out cell 2. Most likely a broken wire strand causing intermittent short. 
- This intermittent nature could explain why the battery was operating nominally for a while, then shorted due to agitation when the operator was connecting the harness for the solenoid test. This short also can explain the heat observed, bad voltage readings, and damage to the PCB.

would_settle_it.what: the ODU solder cups before potting removal, to see the stray strand bridging pins 8 and 9

would_settle_it.file: SharePoint Investigation Report.pptx (LM Overheating HLB, Solenoid Test Cable)
would_settle_it.what: the full teardown photos and pin-by-pin findings

reasoning: The solenoids, test cable and its pinout all checked out with no short. Teardown of the battery found pins 8 and 9 of the 16-pin ODU shorted, shorting cell 2, and the short was reproduced by wiggling the wires behind the ODU. The short disappeared when the potting was removed, so the stray strand was not seen directly, which keeps confidence at medium.
notes: Findings shifted during teardown: Mark first found the 8 pin DF13 melted together, then a wiggle test on 2024-01-23 found no short at ODU pins 8 and 9, then later that day the short was reproduced behind the ODU. The test cable uses pins 7 and 10 only (pinout attachment), so pins 8 and 9 are unused by the cable. The drawing PDFs hold only title block text.

event: Tails 522 and 529 could not connect to the GCS during LM source inspection because their XCOMM boards were stuck in a boot loop; investigation became the systemic SD card corruption study.
failure_mode: SD card file system corruption; the XCOMM SD driver hangs in initialization (timeout handling leads to access violation and watchdog reset loop) so the board never finishes booting
contributing: SD driver initialization timeouts lock up the processor instead of failing gracefully
suspected charge leakage (bit rot) while stored unpowered for months
mixed and possibly lower quality SD card part numbers in use

evidence.quote: 529 XCOMM we removed the SD Card and the XCOMM was able to fully boot and make it to the XCOMM webpage
Code is stuck waiting for a SD Card read in its initialization routine.
there appears to be no connection between randomized power disconnection and SD corruption in the sample of 8 autopilots studied.
Ryan analysis below in the comments shows that the leakage (bit rot) issue is more likely than not the source of our problems, although it is not conclusive.
A corrupt SD Card causes the driver to utilize the timeouts in the initialization code.

team_root_cause:
- SD Card became corrupted. There are many different reasons an SD Card can become corrupted. We know the SD card write operation occurs in blocks every few seconds, if a power event occurred mid-write it could have corrupted the data or the card may have been faulty from the factory.
- Code is stuck waiting for a SD Card read in its initialization routine
- Removing the corrupted SD Card allows boot to succeed.
- Voltage leakage while unpowered and in storage causes a stored bit to flip from 1 to 0 and results in file and file system corruption.

would_settle_it.what: storage history and card part numbers for each corrupted card, to test the unpowered storage theory
vendor failure analysis of the NAND (planned with SanDisk) to tell bit rot from a factory defect

reasoning: On 529 removing the SD card let the XCOMM boot, and the reinstalled card showed corrupted files; reformatting fixed it. A debugger showed the firmware stuck waiting on an SD card read in initialization, and FS2-1661 found the driver timeouts lock the processor. Why the cards corrupted is not settled: a power cycling test found no corruption, and storage leakage is favored but called not conclusive.
notes: Tail 522's XCOMM was only recovered by re-pushing the bootloader; the 522-specific SD removal test is not recorded, so 522 is assigned by the shared symptom. Board 5-5306 had a card that could not be reformatted. Similar cases on 508 and 525. The two rework PDFs have no extractable text. The results spreadsheet export shows 300 of 2894 rows; all shown rows have no SD corruption.

event: An ODU connector backshell broke off with its wires attached during production; investigation found DP100 potting applied late in its working life does not wick between the solder cups.
failure_mode: DP100 cures too fast for large batches, so potting applied after about 3 minutes does not flow to the base of the ODU, leaving a weak bond and a backshell that can unscrew or break off with the wires
contributing: no in-process inspection of potting
no control of potting compound working life or application method
reports of reused mixing tips and untracked mix time
spec sheet working life (5 min) longer than the usable window

evidence.quote: one backshell broke off with wires.
at 4.5 minutes into work life it is already cured enough to make it extremely difficult to use
3 minutes after DP100 is mixed still shows good flow to bottom of ODU regardless of whether applied at top or bottom of cavity, but 4 minutes 30 seconds after mixing shows poor flow.
The backshell of the last connector potted at top of cavity (4.5 minutes into potting compound’s worklife) can be unscrewed by hand

team_root_cause:
- DP100 cures quickly to do large batches of ODUs, resulting in poor flow/wicking between solder cups.
- No in process inspections for potting.
- No controls/procedure checking working life of potting compound, applying potting compound at the bottom of the cup, etc.
- Reports of improper potting techniques (reusing mixing tips, not tracking mix time, etc).
- Working life listing on spec sheet (5 min) of potting compound is longer than the tested applicable window (<3 .5 min).

would_settle_it.what: the broken backshell, to confirm unwicked potting at the solder cups
full test results and photos
which harnesses failed and when they were potted

reasoning: A controlled test potted ODU connectors at 1.5 minute intervals: potting at 3 minutes still flowed to the base, at 4.5 minutes it flowed poorly and that backshell unscrewed by hand. This directly shows the mechanism proposed for the broken backshell. The failed part itself is not described in the export, so the link to that one unit rests on matching symptoms.
notes: Ticket status is Canceled, but the investigation was completed and corrective actions were listed. The branch cable drawing PDF text is extracted mirrored (reversed characters) and is not usable as quoted evidence. No tail number; this is a production harness issue.

event: New production tail 606 showed unstable VTOL altitude behavior during SCO flights (altitude loss of over 70 ft at transition, jumpy landing), which went away after the VTOL AP was replaced.
component: VTOL AP (avionics board assy SN T-S100267)
failure_mode: poor vertical channel control with large CAN baro altitude errors against GPS and LRF in VTOL; fault inside the removed VTOL AP not identified
contributing: baro static port affected by rotor wake in VTOL (fleet-wide, per team)

evidence.quote: The logs show similar discrepancies in baro alt vs. GPS, and were actually a bit worse on this past flight than the previous logs.
Vehicle was flown last Friday with the VTOL AP replaced. All 3 flights were normal, performed the same as other aircraft that day. ADP did not get replaced.
I am not entirely clear on why replacing the VTOL board without the air data system would have improved things since the errors seemed to be in the CAN baro measurements.
VTOL AP was replaced and issue was resolved.
it seems like local flow from the rotors is disrupting the air around the static port.

team_root_cause: Unstable flow of rotor wake causes inaccuracies in baro altimeter measurements when VTOL rotors are active.  The problem did seem worse with 606 and seemed to improve with a new VTOL AP.
disagreement: The team names rotor wake disturbing the baro as the cause, a fleet-wide effect. But the odd behavior repeated on 606 and stopped when only the VTOL AP was swapped ("All 3 flights were normal, performed the same as other aircraft that day. ADP did not get replaced."), and the linked task says "VTOL AP was replaced and issue was resolved." That swap points to something specific to the removed VTOL AP, with rotor wake at most a contributor.

would_settle_it.what: baro altitude against GPS on the 2024-02-12 flights, to compare with the post-swap flights
bench test of the removed board, including its baro handling and CAN interface
baro versus GPS after the swap, to confirm the errors really dropped

reasoning: The baro altitude errors were worse on 606 than on other aircraft and repeated on a second test day. Replacing only the VTOL AP, with the ADP left in place, gave three normal flights, and the investigator confirmed the logs looked much better. That swap test narrows the fault to the removed VTOL AP, but no one tested the board, so the part and mechanism inside it are unknown.
notes: The Vehicle Tail Number field says 604, carried over from the cloned ticket VXEP-263; the description and comments are about 606. The swap result rests on one flight day, so different weather is a remaining alternative.
